name: Aftershave balm / witch hazel
lead: Aftershave is a product applied to the skin after shaving, traditionally an alcohol-based liquid called a splash and now also sold as balms, lotions and gels. Balms are usually alcohol-free and moisturizing, and witch hazel and bay rum are among the oldest aftershave ingredients.[1][2]

Witch hazel is a plant extract used as an astringent for minor skin irritation, including razor burn. Wikipedia reports limited clinical evidence for most of its claimed uses.[3] No trials specifically testing aftershave for razor irritation were found.

paras: Splashes are alcohol-based and typically sting briefly on application; balms are lotion-like, usually alcohol-free and often recommended for dry conditions.[1] Ingredients may include antiseptics such as denatured alcohol or witch hazel, astringents, menthol for a numbing effect, and fragrance.[1]

Witch hazel has long been used topically for acne, minor irritation and razor burn.[3] Native Americans used the leaves and bark, and commercial distilled products were sold from the mid-1800s.[3] Steam-distilled witch hazel water contains little or no tannin; the US regulates it as an over-the-counter external-use product for minor irritation.[3] A 2002 human study of a lotion with 10 percent witch hazel found reduced sunburn redness, but Wikipedia states there is limited clinical evidence for most other claims.[3]

Fragrance ingredients are a recognized cause of contact allergy, and labeling rules in the EU require 26 named fragrance allergens to be listed above set concentrations.[4] In a survey of 1,609 people in a 1987 study, men attributed adverse reactions to cosmetics and toiletries most often to soap, followed by aftershave (22 percent of men's complaints).[5] Alcohol-based products commonly cause brief stinging.[1]
Aftershave balms and witch hazel are discussed in grooming circles as a soothing step after shaving, often alongside advice on ingrown hairs. No forum material suitable for citation was available.
No studies found testing aftershave balm for razor irritation. Related research covers witch hazel's effect on sunburn redness and the prevalence of cosmetic adverse reactions, described above.[3][5]

card.summary: Post-shave splash or balm, often containing witch hazel; widely used to soothe, with limited trial evidence.
card.note: Fragrance and alcohol can irritate or sensitize some skin.

quick.overview:
Aftershave balms and splashes are applied after shaving to soothe skin, and witch hazel is a common ingredient. Splashes are alcohol-based; balms are usually moisturizing.

Clinical evidence for soothing razor burn is limited.
quick.mechanism: Alcohol and witch hazel act as antiseptics and astringents; balms add moisturizers and soothing agents, and menthol gives a cooling sensation.
quick.risks: Alcohol may sting, and fragrance ingredients are a known cause of contact allergy. Witch hazel is regulated as an OTC external-use product in the US.
